entries.title: White Sox officially retire Ozzie Guillen's No. 13
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" target="_blank" >White Sox</a> retired <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/04/03/white-sox-ozzie-guillen-retire-number-13" target="_blank" >Ozzie Guillen’s No. 13</a> on Saturday night.</p><p>There were laughs, some gentle roasts, memories, emotional moments, recollections of 2005 and mentions of family.</p><p>Guillen’s speech even went long, and the Sox’ game against the Guardians started 17 minutes after it was scheduled.</p><p>So, yes, the event perfectly captured Guillen.</p><p>The manager of the Sox’ 2005 World Series champions, Guillen has come to embody the team. He played for them for 13 seasons, managed them for eight mostly successful (but occasionally explosive) years and has become a beloved and honest TV analyst.</p><p>‘‘Isn’t that like the ultimate thing, to be able to be all three of those things for one team?’’ former Sox catcher A.J. Pierzynski told the Sun-Times. ‘‘He’s really lived the dream of any baseball player with one organization.’’</p><p>Guillen has done that despite — and partially because of — his honesty.</p><p>Blunt as a manager and even more forthright as an analyst, Guillen says what he’s thinking. At times, that got him in trouble with the media and contributed to his stint as the manager of the Marlins lasting only a season.</p><p>It’s also something his former Sox players and today’s fans appreciate about him.</p><p>‘‘He literally told you what he was expecting out of you or what he thought of you,’’ former Sox pitcher Mark Buehrle said. ‘‘Whether it was good or bad, you might not have wanted to hear it, but his door was always open. You could walk in at any time. You might not want to hear what he’s going to tell you, but he’s going to tell you the truth.’’</p><p>Sometimes, however, that can lead to bad exits.</p><p>Guillen and then-vice president Ken Williams saw their professional relationship blow up in 2011. Six years after winning a World Series together, Guillen left for Miami to end one of the most productive and tempestuous partnerships in Chicago baseball.</p><p>But time can change perspectives. Guillen looked back thankfully on Williams hiring him before the 2004 season. Guillen, who replaced the laid-back Jerry Manuel, turned 40 that winter and was selected despite his youth and relative inexperience.</p><p>That decision changed the Sox’ trajectory. And Guillen’s life.</p><p>Guillen became the first manager to lead the Sox to multiple postseason appearances and in 2005 joined a small list of Chicago managers and coaches to win a championship, securing his place in the city’s history.</p><p>‘‘I know there were a lot of ups and downs, hate and love,’’ Guillen said. ‘‘Beautiful, nice but ugly, but we got it done. I did everything in my power in my life to make the White Sox team win every day.’’</p><p>As a player and a manager — and even as an analyst — another one of Guillen’s most defining traits is his emotion. He mostly kept that in check Saturday, with a couple of<br>notable exceptions.</p><p>Venezuela has been bruised and beaten by political forces and natural disasters, and Guillen included his home country in the celebration. In conjunction with the festivities, the Sox and Guillen launched the Relief for Venezuela fundraiser to benefit earthquake recovery and relief.</p><p>Wearing pins of the Venezuelan flag on his lapel, Guillen beamed when he spoke about the country’s baseball heritage and how many of its greats wear or wore No. 13. Dave Concepcion, the shortstop for the 1970s ‘‘Big Red Machine’’ that won the 1975 and 1976 World Series, donned No. 13. The Braves’ Ronald Acuna Jr. wears it now.</p><p>No Sox figure will wear it again. The No. 13 is now on display above the first-base line, next to the No. 11 worn by Hall of Fame shortstop and fellow Venezuelan legend Luis Aparicio.</p><p>Aparicio’s son Nelson — yes, named for his father’s longtime double-play partner, Nellie Fox — was visibly stirred when the curtain hiding Guillen’s name and number came down.</p><p>‘‘It’s a dream,’’ Nelson Aparicio told the Sun-Times after watching the ceremony on the field next to the Sox’ third-base dugout. ‘‘Seeing his name besides my father’s name, that’s great. Two Venezuelans from the same organization with their number retired.’’</p><p>Guillen was just glad to live to see his number go up.</p><p>It’s hard to know whether he was joking, but Guillen said that when the topic came up, he would tell his wife, Ibis, that the team was just waiting until he died to retire his No. 13. More seriously, he relished the fact that chairman Jerry Reinsdorf is still around and that former broadcaster Ken ‘‘Hawk’’ Harrelson is, too.</p><p>Then here’s where the emotions really kicked in for Guillen.</p><p>‘‘I’m going to look up and see the last name every day,’’ Guillen said. ‘‘To me, the biggest thrill when I see the number [and] the name out there is what it means to my grandkids to walk to this field and see that. That’s the biggest thrill to me.’’</p><p>Tearing up, Guillen then said he would stop talking about his kids and family to keep himself from crying.</p>

entries.title: ‘We’ve got tired players’ at close of 17 games in 17 days, but Cubs have thrived during challenging stretch
entries.summary: <p>KANSAS CITY – <b>Pete Crow-Armstrong</b> is perhaps baseball’s best defender.</p><p>But for the second time in four games, the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a>’ <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/05/cubs-pete-crow-armstrong-shohei-ohtani-nl-mvp-race-dodgers-playoffs-craig-counsell-shota-imanaga" >MVP candidate</a> was not in his usual spot center field but DH’ing, off his feet once more as the team comes to the end of a stretch of 17 games in 17 days.</p><p>“We’ve got tired players, for sure,” manager <b>Craig Counsell</b> said before Saturday’s game, a 6-3 loss to the Royals.</p><p>It’s a daunting stretch for any team, but in the face of such a physical challenge, the Cubs have thrived, going 11-5 with one game remaining before Monday’s off day.</p><p>The Cubs came into Saturday tops in the NL with a .770 OPS, 144 hits and 81 runs scored since the stretch began July 24.</p><p>Their <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/07/30/cubs-mlb-trade-deadline-pitching-starting-rotation-matthew-boyd-shota-imanaga-colin-rea-david-peterson-javier-assad-tarik-skubal" >starting pitching was particularly impressive</a>, with a 2.65 ERA that ranked second in the NL. Remove <b>Jameson Taillon</b>’s seven-run clunker in his final game with the Cubs, and that number was down to 2.03, second best in baseball.</p><p>In the thick of it all, the Cubs went through an eventful trade deadline, which saw <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/03/cubs-mlb-trade-deadline-jed-hoyer-top-prospects-trades-kevin-gausman-clay-holmes-ryan-zeferjahn-braxton-garrett-tyrone-taylor" >an aggressive front office</a> try to best position them for a deep October run, and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/04/cubs-dodgers-three-peat-world-series-favorites-tarik-skubal-dansby-swanson" >a raucous sweep of the juggernaut Dodgers</a>.</p><p>“This was 17 in a row. For most teams, that’s their longest stretch of the season,” Counsell said. “It happened at a time in the season where the trade deadline’s around it, which creates a lot around the team. Some hot weather in multiple cities that you play in, you always worry about it.</p><p>“We’ve handled the first 15 games exceptionally well, especially our starting pitching has been outstanding for this stretch and, to me, the key to this. That’s what can go wrong in [a stretch like this] more than anything, [impacting the bullpen], and they’ve been excellent.”</p><p><b>Happ gets ahold of one</b></p><p>Left fielder <b>Ian Happ</b> has been struggling at the plate, coming into Saturday hitting just .162 with a sub-.300 on-base percentage and only one home run in his previous 34 games. A four-strikeout game Friday was particularly ugly.</p><p>But he got off the schneid Saturday, snapping an 0-for-22 stretch at the dish by homering for the first time since July 20, later adding a double.</p><p>“For us to be the best team we can be,” Counsell said before the game, “we need Ian Happ to be a good player.”</p><p>That the dinger came off a righty won’t make his splits any less dramatic; he came into Saturday with a .798 OPS against right-handers versus a .517 OPS against left-handers.</p><p>But it was a positive result for an important Cubs hitter.</p><p>“A very good night, he’ll sleep good,” Counsell said after the game. “Hopefully, we’re getting the good Ian back. It’s been frustrating for him, but this is a good hitter, this is a guy who’s having a good year against right-handed pitching. He’s going to do good things for us.”</p><p><b>Holmes rusty in return</b></p><p>Newly acquired right-hander <b>Clay Holmes</b> made his Cubs debut Saturday, his first time on a major league mound since May 15, when he went on the injured list with a fractured fibula.</p><p>It didn’t go too great, with Holmes tagged for four runs in four innings of work.</p><p>A brief outing was not entirely unexpected, given the long layoff.</p><p>“It took a lot of work to get back to this point, and it definitely felt good to be back in a big league game,” Holmes said. “Obviously, that’s not the full goal. You want to be back and helping this team win games. I just wasn’t quite sharp enough tonight.”</p>

entries.title: Family of man whose body was at South Chicago Chapel told his body can be released
entries.summary: <p>As the Cook County medical examiner’s office works to identify the 56 bodies removed from a South Side funeral home, the family of Keith Allen Young learned Saturday his body can be released, his sister said.</p><p>The update brings Young’s family a step closer to paying their respects. His body, which they thought was being prepared by South Chicago Chapel for burial, never arrived at the church for his wake on Thursday.</p><p>Young's funeral was supposed to be Friday. Instead, his family went to the medical examiner’s office to see what they could find out.</p><p>Stephanie Young said the medical examiner’s office contacted one of her brothers Saturday to say their brother's body had been identified. She believes the next step is for the family to find another funeral home that can receive her brother’s body.</p><p>“It’s just the devastation to our family to have to redo this whole situation over again,” Young said. “At this point, we’re just happy to have his body ... so we can move forward in laying him to rest.”</p><p>Keith Allen Young, 48, died July 26. His body <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/08/07/south-side-funeral-home-bodies-families-investigation" target="_blank" ><u>was delivered</u></a> Wednesday to South Chicago Chapel, 2939 E. 95th St., the same day the business had its license revoked, as previously reported by the Sun-Times.</p><p>The funeral home was supposed to prepare his body and deliver it to a church Thursday, but it never arrived.</p><p>Young’s relatives said their calls to the funeral home seeking answers were not returned, and the family learned through the media that the funeral home had been shut down.</p><p>The medical examiner’s office said Friday it had taken jurisdiction of 56 remains from the funeral home and was working to assess their condition, confirm identification and ensure appropriate paperwork was filed.</p><p>The office could not confirm Saturday how many of the remains had been identified so far or provide additional updates on the process.</p><p>Additional information was expected Monday morning, according to Natalia Derevyanny, spokesperson for the medical examiner’s office.</p><p>Young's bodies and others were found on Thursday by police. Officers went to the chapel that day learning that bodies at the South Deering funeral home were not being stored at or below 40 degrees, as required by state regulations, according to a police report obtained by the Chicago Sun-Times. Inside, officers found dozens of bodies in various areas of the funeral home. The bodies were not refrigerated and were in various stages of decomposition, according to the report.<br></p>

entries.title: Sophie Cunningham draws dueling protests outside Sky-Fever game
entries.summary: <p>Here was the scene outside the United Center on Saturday: On one side of Madison Street, a group had gathered to “Support Sophie,” with a cardboard cutout of Fever guard <b>Sophie Cunningham</b> and T-shirts bearing XX and XY chromosomes.</p><p>A few yards away, counterprotesters waved rainbow and transgender flags and wore shirts reading “Protect Trans Kids.”</p><p>Why outside a Fever-<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky</a> game?</p><p>Cunningham has become a flashpoint in the debate over transgender participation in women’s sports. In an ESPN profile, she said she had received criticism for “hating trans,” which she denied.</p><p>“I think that I am here to extend love,” Cunningham said. “But I also think that love is truth, being honest. And I want to protect young girls in a locker room, or young girls in sport who shouldn’t have to go against biological men.”</p><p>Since the All-Star break, groups advocating to exclude transgender women from women’s sports have rallied outside Fever road games.</p><p><b>Amy Sousa</b>, who helped organize the first rally in Seattle, said she hadn’t ever watched the WNBA but now wants to support Cunningham.</p><p>“This whole thing has taken off,” she said. ”We’re here to be completely pro women, pro girl. Our basic stance is that women and girls sports need to be designated, as science says, on the basis of sex.”</p><p>Across Madison, others came specifically to support transgender athletes.</p><p>“Youth sports saved my life,” said one long-time Sky fan, who asked not to be named. “It’s hard enough feeling like a kid who feels different than everyone else. Not having a space in sports would have been so harmful to me.</p><p>“Which young girls is Cunningham trying to protect, and from who? I think that young girls in sports need protection from a lot of other things. There are so many trans kids who need to be lifted up and not torn down.”</p><p>They noted cyberbullying and ACL injuries as two things young girls actually need protection from.</p><p><b>WNBPA weighs in</b></p><p>The players union addressed the debate Friday, saying: “Hate, abuse, and demonization of any person or group of people, including transgender people, only fuel fear, division, and harm. We will continue to have hard conversations. But we will not be used as political pawns.”</p><p>WNBPA secretary <b>Elizabeth Williams</b> told the Sun-Times that especially when it comes to the conversation around trans athletes, people try to use WNBA players to advance their agendas.</p><p>“We just want to make sure that we’re recentering the focus back on protecting Title IX,” Williams said. “Protecting girls in sport. That’s always been our priority.”</p><p><b>Fouling around </b></p><p>Inside the arena, Sky guard <b>DiJonai Carrington</b> was ejected for a Flagrant 2 foul on Cunningham, and <b>Natasha Cloud</b> received a technical in the fourth quarter.</p><p><b>Caitlin Clark</b> was assessed a technical in the third quarter that would have triggered a one-game suspension. The WNBA rescinded it after the game.</p>
entries.author: Alissa Hirsh

entries.title: DiJonai Carrington ejected after hard foul on Sophie Cunningham as Sky fall to Fever
entries.summary: <p>It was a jumbled affair at the United Center, even by the standards of this <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky</a> season.</p><p>Outside the arena, dueling protests had formed around Fever guard Sophie Cunningham’s recent comments opposing transgender women participating in women’s sports. Inside, a game moved from Wintrust Arena to accommodate a bigger crowd felt more like Gainbridge Fieldhouse West than a home game for the Sky.</p><p>And in the middle of it all, the Sky lost another close one, 90-86.</p><p>The Fever gave their traveling fans plenty to cheer about early. Caitlin Clark put on a show, making all the right reads and hitting 5-of-6 from deep. The Sky looked sluggish, missing layups and offering little resistance.</p><p>Then DiJonai Carrington checked in.</p><p>Carrington, who missed the first half of the season recovering from foot surgery, has changed the Sky’s energy since returning. She did it almost immediately Saturday, scoring eight points in three minutes and helping turn an early deficit into a lead.</p><p>But it didn’t last.</p><p>Cunningham broke free in transition, and Carrington chased her down from behind. Carrington went for the block but caught Cunningham across the head and neck, sending her hard to the floor.</p><p>Cunningham popped back up and gave Carrington a little shove. Words followed before teammates and security separated them.</p><p>After review, Carrington was assessed a Flagrant 2 and ejected. Cunningham was not given a technical. Officials later said they “deemed her reaction to the severity of the contact to be acceptable.”</p><p>Minutes later, Carrington posted “WHITE PRIVILEGE” on Threads and tagged the Fever.</p><p>Neither coach thought the foul was intentional. Fever coach Stephanie White, who coached Carrington in Connecticut, and Sky coach Tyler Marsh both said they saw Carrington making a play on the ball.</p><p>Cunningham took the opposite stance.</p><p>She said she “absolutely” believed Carrington fouled her intentionally, adding that she has “no beef” with Carrington but believes she has “some pent-up stuff.”</p><p>“So, get your s— off,” Cunningham said. “That’s fine. I can take it.”</p><p>There is some history here, although not directly between Cunningham and Carrington.</p><p>One of the moments that helped build Cunningham’s reputation as Clark’s “enforcer” came last season against the Sun. After Clark and current Sky guard Jacy Sheldon, longtime Big Ten rivals at Iowa and Ohio State, tangled earlier in the game, Cunningham later put Sheldon in a headlock during a fastbreak.</p><p>Cunningham acknowledged the parallel, but balked at Carrington getting involved.</p><p>“I did that last year. Yeah, it’s intentional, but [Carrington] wasn’t even on the team,” Cunningham said. “She has no reason to be doing any of that… Good way to get her kicked out.”</p><p>“I do know when people play the Fever, we’re nationally televised, there’s a lot of eyes on us,” Cunningham said. “People just want attention. That’s her just trying to get attention.”</p><p>Asked about Carrington’s “WHITE PRIVILEGE” post, Cunningham dismissed race as a factor.</p><p>“This has nothing to do with race,” Cunningham said. “Last year I did the same thing. I got kicked out, as I deserved to be kicked out. There’s no reason to even play that card.”</p><p>The exchange only added to the controversy already swirling around Cunningham, whose comments about transgender women in sports had followed the Fever from city to city.</p><p>“I want to protect young girls in a locker room, or young girls in sport who shouldn’t have to go against biological men,” Cunningham said in a recent ESPN interview.</p><p>She has since called that position “common sense.” Her comments have spurred rallies outside Fever games from groups such as XX-XY Athletics, which argues that it is “unfair and dangerous to allow males to compete in girls’ and women’s sports.”</p><p>There was also a counterprotest in support of transgender athletes outside the United Center on Saturday.</p><p>Marsh said none of it gave the Sky any more “juice” than usual. With their playoff chances dwindling, he said their focus remains on basketball.</p><p>“We’re just locked in on hoops, really,” Sheldon said. “We come to every game kind of the same, locked in on the scouting report, what we want to get done and ultimately try to win and play good basketball. So that was just our focus. There was no conversation outside of that.”</p><p>One thing that kept the Sky from playing their best basketball was losing Carrington early.</p><p>They were already without leading scorer Sydney Taylor, sidelined by a groin injury. Then they lost one of their best perimeter defenders and most aggressive shot creators after three minutes.</p><p>In a game decided by four points, that hurt.</p>

entries.summary: <p>A fire in an abandoned building in Little Village Saturday night was extinguished in about an hour, according to Chicago police and fire officials.</p><p>Police and firefighters responded to the fire about 7:30 p.m. in the 2200 block of South Lawndale Avenue, police said. entries.title: White Sox add Hagen Smith and Tanner McDougal, beat Guardians to restore three-game AL Central lead
entries.summary: <p>Getting the call to the major leagues was an emotional moment for new <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" target="_blank" >White Sox</a> pitchers <b>Tanner McDougal</b> and <b>Hagen Smith</b>. But as two of the Sox’ top prospects, they understand their assignment is much more than being feel-good stories.</p><p>‘‘I’m excited to go out there and compete and hopefully help win a pennant back here,’’ said McDougal, the Sox’ No. 4 prospect, according to MLB Pipeline.</p><p>There’s still some time before the Sox can do that, but they gave themselves some breathing room in the American League Central race Saturday by beating the Guardians 6-3. The Sox snapped a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/08/07/white-sox-manager-will-venable-appears-to-make-one-of-the-gaffes-of-the-season-in-key-game-against-guardians" target="_blank" >season-high four-game losing streak</a> and restored their three-game lead over the Guardians and Twins in the division.</p><p>‘‘It’s obviously a very important series, so I’m really glad that we got to win this one,’’ said first baseman <b>Munetaka Murakami</b>, who homered in the Sox’ five-run sixth that overturned a 2-0 deficit. ‘‘We were in a bad losing streak right here, so it’s good to reset and then come back today with a win.’’</p><p>Neither McDougal nor Smith, the team’s No. 2 prospect, were used Saturday, but they will be relievers. Both have had injuries this season and were working out of the bullpen at Triple-A Charlotte despite having starting pedigrees.</p><p>And both will be tested in a race that might go down to the last days of the season.</p><p>‘‘It’s awesome,’’ Smith said. ‘‘To go out there and compete is the biggest thing for me. Love going out there and [competing] and [going] out there and [attacking] the hitters.’’</p><p>To make room for McDougal and Smith, the Sox sent left-hander <b>Noah Schultz</b> and right-hander <b>David Sandlin</b> to Charlotte. They also designated right-hander <b>Wikelman Gonzalez</b> for assignment.</p><h3>The Schultz plan</h3><p>Schultz will be a starter in the minors. Sox manager <b>Will Venable</b> said there are some mechanical issues Schultz needs to iron out.</p><p>Right-hander <b>Erick Fedde</b>, who was dropped from the rotation after the Sox acquired <b>Luis Castillo</b> from the Mariners at the trade deadline, is a candidate to make the next start in Schultz’s spot. Venable didn’t definitively anoint Fedde a starter again because the Sox still might need him out of the bullpen in the next few days.</p><h3>The gaffe</h3><p>Venable still wasn’t over his blunder Friday that forced Schultz from the game when he made a second mound visit in the first inning. Venable said he didn’t sleep well afterward, probably would lose sleep for a couple of more nights and wasn’t OK yet with what happened.</p><p>He also knew he needed to look forward.</p><p>‘‘That’s what this league is about: You’ve got to dust yourself off and get back up and go to battle,’’ Venable said. ‘‘So that’s what we’re going to do.’’</p>

entries.title: How Blackhawks rookie Anton Frondell is preparing to play center in the NHL
entries.summary: <p>Anton Frondell has an opportunity to be the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a>' first-line center, at least for the first month of the season during Connor Bedard's absence.</p><p>The 19-year-old Swedish forward personally hasn't given much thought to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/07/26/projecting-blackhawks-lines-patrick-kane-bowen-byram-connor-bedard-frank-nazar" target="_blank" >what line</a> he will play on. But he has spent his entire summer thinking about and preparing for his new position.</p><p>His tryout at center at the end of last season came unexpectedly, since he had played exclusively on the wing for his Swedish club, Djurgardens. He <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/04/01/blackhawks-anton-frondell-video-breakdown-center-jonathan-toews" target="_blank" >showed promise</a> in his first 12 NHL games, nine of which were spent at center, by recording nine points. But he also struggled on faceoffs and missed some defensive assignments.</p><p>By the time the puck drops for the Hawks' 2026-27 season opener Sept. 29 at the Golden Knights, he should look more comfortable at center.</p><p>"You need to know the whole game and how to play the role in the middle," Frondell said Friday on the phone from Sweden, where he was driving home to a hearty pasta dinner.</p><p>"I'm trying to study it, watch a couple players and look deep into faceoffs and how to try to win more."</p><p>Panthers star Aleksander Barkov has long been Frondell's idol, so the fact he's one of the most dominant two-way centers in the world made him an obvious choice to feature in Frondell's video sessions this summer. Frondell also got to face Barkov on the ice for the first time in an exhibition game before the world championships in May.</p><p>At the dot, Frondell (who won only 30.2% of his faceoffs in those 12 games) has an extremely long way to go to catch Barkov (56.9% over his last two healthy seasons). But after studying Barkov, he thinks his sheer strength could be an advantage.</p><p>"Faceoffs is a lot of timing, a lot of reacting quick to when the puck drops, and then if you're strong and you have a lot of power in your faceoffs, you can win a lot of them," Frondell said. "That's a way for me to win more: with my power."</p><p>It's worth noting Frondell's weight has held steady at 209 pounds for the past year. Unlike many other Hawks forward prospects, he has already filled out his 6-1 frame and then some. He is undoubtedly a power forward, which makes him something of a unicorn within the Hawks' young core.</p><p>At his size, increasing quickness and explosiveness must be higher priorities, which Frondell realized upon joining the Hawks in March.</p><p>"[With] the style of hockey and the rink I'm used to — the Swedish size — the game is a little bit different, and I could see that right away when I got to play a couple NHL games," he said. </p><p>"[In Sweden], you can save your speed or use your glide a little bit. In the NHL, it felt like everything was tighter. As a center in the D-zone, you need to get out to the corner quick, then get back in front of the net, [then] maybe to the other corner."</p><p>During Frondell's 2024-25 draft year, his skating was considered a weakness, but the Hawks were <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2025/07/13/blackhawks-anton-frondell-nhl-draft-prospects-marcus-kruger-johnny-oduya-sweden" target="_blank" >less concerned about it</a> than other teams because they could tell how hard he was working to improve it — and how steadily it was improving as a result.</p><p>That trend has continued this summer, which Frondell has spent doing sprints in the gym and then translating those movements onto the ice.</p><p>"I feel like when I'm at my top speed, I can use it," he said. "But I want to get into my speed faster so I can earn time and space in the first couple steps."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">🚨ANTON FRONDELL FIRST NHL GOAL🚨 <a href="https://t.co/8AEuLEIg74">pic.twitter.com/8AEuLEIg74</a></p>— Blackhawks on CHSN (@CHSN_Blackhawks) <a href="https://x.com/CHSN_Blackhawks/status/2039143453645295620?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">April 1, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>He certainly hasn't slacked training-wise. He took only about a week off after the world championships before resuming light skating with brothers William Eklund (Sharks) and Victor Eklund (Islanders), two close friends. </p><p>Then he ramped up his on-ice work with a group of players including Tom Willander (Canucks), a summer training partner for the last several years. </p><p>Since last week, Frondell — along with the Eklunds and Viggo Bjorck (Jets) — have been practicing with Djurgardens, whose first exhibition game is Thursday. The NHL-bound kids won't play in any games, but they will go through an entire training camp before NHL camps begin in September.</p><p>"For us, it's perfect," Frondell said. "When everything starts, we'll already have a feeling for team practice. [We'll have] been going into battles and all that stuff."</p><p>Bjorck, at the NHL draft combine in June, described Frondell as a "more calm version of Victor," and he is certainly low-strung and lighthearted for being such a competitive, driven person.</p><p>He's not fazed by much, including the lofty expectations for his official NHL rookie season: he's tied for fourth in preseason Calder Trophy odds, per FanDuel.</p><p>Perhaps Frondell's affinity for tennis contributes to that zen mindset. Tennis allows him to escape the hockey bubble, get outdoors and appreciate the simplicity when it's "just you and the racket," as he described last summer.</p><p>Both his dad, Henrik, and his older sister, Alva, played tennis competitively, and they still spend several hours each week dueling on a clay court near their summer house.</p><p>"It's just a fun thing to do and think about something else," Frondell said Friday. "And at the same time, getting some training [with] hand-eye [coordination] and footwork."</p><p>When the idea of soon becoming teammates with Patrick Kane pops into Frondell's head, though, some excitement does penetrate his easygoing attitude.</p><p>"Growing up, you watch every highlight of him, every YouTube video you could find, and now I have the chance to sit in the same room as him," he said. "It's pretty cool and nothing I thought I would ever do."</p><p>Kane has mentioned Frank Nazar as a possible linemate during Bedard's absence, and Kane and Nazar's chemistry from skating together this summer could be a point in Nazar's favor.</p><p>But Frondell's attentiveness to defense — even if his defensive execution and analytics didn't quite match his effort this spring — as well as his deadly shot and ability to protect the puck and hold off opponents could make sense next to Kane, too.</p><p>The Hawks will have time, albeit not a lot, to experiment with these combinations during camp. Frondell hopes to leap into that process with as little rust as possible.</p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Lifeline Thrown to Nephew Instead Weighs Down Relatives
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I suggested to my husband that he invite his nephew "Ryan" (age 26) to stay with us. Ryan definitely needed some male direction. He was homeless, jobless and didn't even know how to apply for a job. Ryan is not mentally challenged. He simply was never taught anything until he was thrown out on the street with no skills.</p><p>Once Ryan moved in, I realized just how big a mistake we had made. He got a job because a relative was able to get him hired without even so much as an interview. He doesn't make enough money to move out on his own. He sleeps all day and plays video games all night anytime he's not at work.</p><p>Ryan doesn't shower, doesn't do his own laundry and leaves dirty dishes all over the room he sleeps in. The room smells horrible. On top of that, my clothes closet is in that room. (There is no other option for my clothes.) I'm worried his body odor and dirty clothes will soon make all my clothes smell as well.</p><p>This was meant to be a temporary situation until Ryan had saved enough to get his own place. However, he makes no effort to save toward that end. I wouldn't intervene if it weren't that he is diminishing my quality of life. I was all in for helping him out, but I can no longer live under these conditions. My husband keeps saying he'll handle it but doesn't. It's not my place because Ryan is his relative. I'm in desperate need of your wisdom. — <i>SMELLY SITUATION</i></p><p><b>DEAR SMELLY SITUATION:</b> Ryan's parents did their son a terrible disservice by not teaching him survival skills so he could live independently. Because you chose to take him off the streets, that task now falls to you. I say "you" because your husband doesn't appear to have the backbone to address this. Both of you need to tell Ryan there are rules he must follow if he wants to continue living with you.</p><p>Show him how to put his clothes (and detergent) into a washing machine and to use the dryer. Tell him he must shower at least three times a week and use deodorant every day. No longer tolerate food in his room or dirty dishes left in the sink. He must eat in the dining area like a civilized person.</p><p>Also, set up a savings plan for what little money he earns so part of his paycheck can accumulate and he can finally move out on his own — even if it's with a roommate. If he learns the lessons that you teach him, someone may actually be willing to share quarters with him. I wish you luck. Nothing will change until you assert yourself.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My son and I have been estranged for three years. He wants nothing more to do with me. I do not expect to see him ever again. However, I still have items of his. Do I pack up the items and have them dropped off, or what? I'm not sure what to do. — <i>EX-MOTHER IN ARIZONA</i></p><p><b>DEAR EX-MOTHER:</b> If you are sure that your son is still living at the same address, box the items up and send them. That way, you can never be blamed for withholding anything from him.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren, also known as Jeanne Phillips, and was founded by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 69440, Los Angeles, CA 90069.</i></p>

entries.title: Toddler, man critically injured in South Shore house fire
entries.summary: <p>A 1-year-old boy and a 29-year-old man were critically injured in a South Shore residential fire Saturday night, Chicago police said.</p><p>Officers and Chicago firefighters responded to the accidental fire around 6:30 p.m. in the 6800 block of South Merrill Avenue, according to police.</p><p>Three people were injured. The 1-year-old was taken to Comer Children's Hospital; the man in critical condition and a 26-year-old woman who suffered minor burns were both taken to University of Chicago Medical Center, police said.</p><p>The Chicago Fire Department is investigating the cause of the fire.</p>

entries.title: Woman killed in Lake View hit-and-run crash
entries.summary: <p>A pedestrian was fatally struck by a driver Saturday night while trying to cross Irving Park Road in Lake View, Chicago police said.</p><p>The 25-year-old woman was walking between two parked cars in the 1400 block of Irving Park Road around 9:20 p.m. when a driver in a sedan hit her, police said.</p><p>The driver fled west and crashed into an SUV, which then hit a black sedan. The driver of the SUV tried to detain him, but he got back into his car and fled again. He then crashed into a tree, according to police. He got out of the car and ran off, then entering a building in the 4000 block of North Ashland Avenue, police said.</p><p>He was later arrested and charges are pending.</p><p>The woman was taken to Advocate Illinois Masonic Medical Center where she was later pronounced dead, according to police. The drivers of the two cars that were hit declined medical attention.</p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: 4 hurt in Austin drive-by shooting
entries.summary: <p>Three people were shot Sunday morning in the Austin neighborhood, Chicago police said.</p><p>They were standing outside around 8:20 a.m. in the 1400 block of North Leclaire Avenue when a white sedan pulled up and someone inside fired several shots. Three of the four people were shot: A 33-year-old woman shot in the knee and ankle, a 36-year-old man shot in the leg and foot, and a 43-year-old man was shot several times. A 30-year-old woman wasn't shot but suffered injuries to her feet.</p><p>All four were taken to Stroger Hospital in fair condition.</p><p>No one has been arrested, according to police.</p>

entries.title: Bears' Sunday practice delayed by lightning near Halas Hall, fans sent home
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> will be late getting on the field Sunday and few will be watching when they do.</p><p>As players were loosening up for a 12:30 p.m. practice, alarms went off for lightning in the area and they were called back to the building. Shortly after, the team dismissed fans and decided the practice will be closed to the public.</p><p>The Bears have mostly avoided weather-related issues in the first few weeks of training camp. One other practice was closed to fans at the last minute, but the team still was able to get its full session in on time and outside.</p><p>The team has not said what time practice will begin.</p><p>After this, the Bears are holding their <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/07/15/bears-to-practice-at-stevenson-high-school-as-part-of-training-camp" >“Varsity Bears” walk-through</a> Monday morning at nearby Stevenson High School, then have an off day before a stretch of practices leading up their preseason opener Sunday against the Browns at Soldier Field.</p>

entries.title: No. 9 Bolingbrook has the talent and experience to compete with private school powers
entries.summary: <p>Bolingbrook, ranked No. 9 in the preseason Super 25, finished last season just one successful two-point conversion away from reaching the Class 8A semifinals.</p><p>A load of high-level talent and 18 players who started games are back. The Raiders ended last season as one of the best teams in the state, despite battling special teams woes throughout the campaign.</p><p>“We lost so many extra points because we had inconsistency with our kicker,” Bolingbrook coach Titcus Pettigrew said. “Now we have a full-time kicker, and we are putting our best 11 on special teams. It has been the top priority. Everyone has bought in, and we are going to make sure we win that facet of the game.”</p><p>Bolingbrook may be the only public school in the area that can match the Catholic League powers for raw size and ability. Defensive end Darieon Prescott (6-4, 255 pounds) recently committed to Notre Dame and is a consensus top-20 talent in the national class of 2028. Senior running back TJ Lewis, an Oklahoma State recruit, scored 22 TDs last season and accounted for 1,808 total yards.</p><p>Junior defensive back Antoine Norfleet has an offer from Illinois, and junior running back Jordan Donald holds an offer from Kansas State. Almost a half dozen other players are expected to impress and earn Power Four offers over the course of the season.</p><p>“We have a lot of dogs out here that are going to get recruited,” Lewis said. entries.title: 3 killed in separate overnight shootings in Chicago
entries.summary: <p>Six people were shot early Sunday on Chicago's South and West sides — three of whom died from their injuries and two were critically wounded, Chicago police said.</p><p>First responders found a man in New City unresponsive and suffering from several gunshot wounds around midnight, police said. He was pronounced dead at the scene in the 4500 block of South Honore Street.</p><p>Just before 2 a.m. in Austin, a 32-year-old man was found fatally shot in the 300 block of South Kilpatrick Avenue, police said. The man, who was shot in his temple, was pronounced dead at the scene.</p><p>About 20 minutes later, a 29-year-old man was standing outside a car in Little Village when a person drove passed and shot him in the head, according to police. He was pronounced dead at the scene in the 2800 block of South Kedzie Avenue.</p><p>No additional details about any of the deaths were reported.</p><p>Three people were shot in the Garfield Park neighborhood around 1:45 a.m. Officers responding to a call for shots fired found a 45-year-old man unresponsive in the 3400 block of West Carroll Avenue. The man, suffering from gunshot wounds to his arm and hip, was taken in critical condition to Mount Sinai Hospital.</p><p>Two people later walked into Mount Sinai with injuries from the same shooting, police said. One of them, a 46-year-old man, is in critical condition suffering from several gunshot wounds to his leg. The other, a 34-year-old man, is in fair condition with a gunshot to his knee, police said.</p><p>No arrests have been made in any of the shootings, according to police.</p>

entries.title: White Sox lefty Hagen Smith, team's No. 2 prospect, making major-league debut
entries.summary: <p>Hagen Smith, the White Sox' second-ranked prospect, is making his major-league debut after a rain delay Sunday against the Guardians.</p><p>The Sox drafted Smith out of Arkansas with their first-round pick in 2024. This season at Triple-A Charlotte, Smith is 1-6 with a 4.32 ERA in 20 games (14 starts). In 58 1/3 innings, he has allowed 39 hits and 40 walks with 87 strikeouts. Smith has held hitters to a .189 batting average.</p>

entries.title: Why the Bears' QB room is the best in a shuffled NFC North
entries.summary: <p>When Lions coach Dan Campbell announced Sunday that second-string quarterback Teddy Bridgewater had decided to retire, his mind flashed back six years. When Campbell was the Saints’ tight ends coach, Drew Brees hurt his thumb when he whacked the Rams’ Aaron Donald on his follow-through. Bridgewater took over as the starter for five weeks — including a 36-25 thumping of the Bears at Soldier Field.</p><p>“We lost him for five weeks and Teddy stepped in and we won five in a row, man. …” Campbell said. “He’s going to be missed.”</p><p>In the modern NFL, everyone needs a reliable backup quarterback — and a strong quarterback room to support the starter.</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> don’t have the best starting quarterback in the NFC North, though they hope Caleb Williams continues to trend upward. Bridgewater’s retirement Sunday, though, only strengthens the argument that the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/08/06/bears-training-camp-report-day-8-qb-caleb-williams-sharper-bryson-graham-nfl-bulls" target="_blank" >Bears</a> have the best quarterback room in the division.</p><p>The combination of Williams and second-stringer Tyson Bagent tops the other three duos.</p><p>The Lions’ Jared Goff ranked second in the NFL in passing yard and third in passer rating last year. The Lions scrambled to sign another passer, adding Josh Dobbs, who last year threw 10 passes for the Patriots. Former U of I standout Luke Altmayer is on the team as an undrafted free agent.</p><p>The Packers’ Jordan Love was sixth in the NFL in passer rating last year. His backup though, went to Miami this offseason. Malik Willis, who was 2-1 as the starter over the past two seasons, signed a three-year, $67.5 million deal, with $45 million guaranteed, in March. The Packers turned to Tyrod Taylor, a 37-year-old who was drafted when Williams was just 9 years old, as their second-stringer. Second-year quarterback Kyle McCord and Virginia Tech rookie Kyron Drones are their backups; neither has taken am NFL snap.</p><p>Then there are the Vikings — who, despite having three former first-round picks, have the most question marks in the NFC North. They signed former Cardinals No. 1 overall pick Kyler Murray to a one-year deal to fight J.J. McCarthy, their own former first-round pick, for the starting job. Murray has played more first-team snaps during training camp and is considered the favorite to win the job. Murray played five games last year before getting hurt, then benched, then cut.</p><p>McCarthy is staring down a “bust” label after missing all his rookie year because of a knee injury and struggling in Year 2. Since 2020, there have been 39 quarterbacks who have thrown at least 100 passes in their first 10 NFL games. McCarthy’s 72.6 passer rating ranks 31<sup>st</sup>.</p><p>Carson Wentz is the Vikings’ third-stringer, Max Brosmer their fourth-stringer. Wentz went 2-3 as the Vikings’ starter last year, while Brosmer had a passer rating of 53.</p><p>The Bears know that Caleb Williams’ remarkable ability to avoid injury — he’s taken every relevant snap during his two years in the NFL — won’t last forever. They believe in Bagent, whom they gave a two-year, $10 million extension last year to keep him under contract through 2027. Bagent had the best play of practice Sunday, throwing a deep touchdown pass to a diving Kaden Davis. The Bears ended practice 5 seconds later.</p><p>Bagent is wired like Bears head coach Ben Johnson — intense and particular.</p><p>“Usually, if Tyson makes the mistake, it's fixed,” tight end Cole Kmet said. “He's not making that same mistake again. And Ben and the rest of the coaching staff, I know they really appreciate guys like that.”</p><p>The Bears take pride in the continuity inside their quarterbacks room, too. The team’s top three quarterbacks — Williams, Bagent and Case Keenum — are in their second season together, alongside quarterbacks coach J.T. Barrett. Press Taylor, their new offensive coordinator, was the pass-game coordinator last season. Only rookie quarterback Miller Moss, Williams’ former USC teammate, is new.</p><p>That support system helps Williams.</p><p>“Those guys have seen so much football — let alone, they've all been together here,” Taylor said. “So we all have, ‘Hey, remember Week 7 last year when this came up and we did this? Are we still doing that? Or do we want to do something different? Because Week 13, we got the same thing, we changed it based on whatever we want.’</p><p>“You have shared experience to pull from and be able to communicate through.”</p><p>The Bears can plow through their plans a lot faster. Last year, Taylor said, he had to worry about teaching the names of formations and pre-snap motions. Now the conversations are about mastering cadence or adding wrinkles to plays.</p><p>Taylor will get to see how the quarterbacks handle things against an opposing defense later this week. Williams doesn’t figure to play in Saturday’s preseason opener against the Browns at Soldier Field. It would be surprising if Bagent played much. Keenum and Moss, though, should have plenty of chances.</p><p>“They're all taking the next step,” Taylor said. “Having those guys be on the same page and be moving forward together is really special for us.”</p>

entries.title: Guardians-White Sox series finale delayed by rain in second inning
entries.summary: <p>After trying to play through the rain, the umpires gave up. Before the start of the second inning, they called for the tarp.</p><p>The White Sox' series finale against the Guardians Sunday at Rate Field is being delayed by rain, raising the question of whether it should've started at all. Storms to the north canceled the Bears' training-camp practice, which was open to the public. They made their way south, first as a steady rain through which the umpires kept play moving, then as a gusher that brought out the tarp.</p><p>Before then, Sox starter Davis Martin had another rough first inning, allowing two runs (one earned). Guardians leadoff man Steven Kwan extended his on-base streak to 25 games with a single. After advancing to second on Chase DeLauter's walk, Kwan reached third on Jose Ramirez's single and scored on Sox right fielder Braden Montgomery's fielding error. DeLauter then scored on Nathaniel Lowe's sacrifice fly.</p><p>The Sox got one back against Joey Cantillo, but it should've been more. Brenton Doyle led off with a single, stole second and scored on Munetaka Murakami's double. Miguel Vargas dropped a double in front of a diving DeLauter in right field, but Murakami had to hold and stopped at third. Cantillo then struck out Randal Grichuk, Montgomery and Colson Montgomery. </p>

entries.title: Bohemian National Cemetery under investigation for improperly stored remains, equipment failures
entries.summary: <p>The Illinois comptroller's office announced it’s investigating Bohemian National Cemetery after a tip last month led investigators to find equipment failures and remains being improperly stored.</p><p>Investigators from the state comptroller’s office visited the North Park cemetery the morning after the July 22 tip and found “multiple equipment failures and some human remains waiting to be cremated that were not maintained at the proper temperature,” according to a statement the comptroller's office issued Saturday.</p><p>The 35 remains have been cremated and returned to the respective families, the office said.</p><p>Bohemian National Cemetery Association was ordered to stop accepting decedents until the issues were resolved, which the state office said it has complied with so far. It could face fines, probation or suspension of its crematory authority license, according to a comptroller’s office spokesperson. </p><p>Bohemian National Cemetery Association didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. The comptroller’s office said the cemetery’s visiting and operating hours are not affected by the investigation.</p><p>This comes a few days after a South Side funeral home, run by Johanna and Clark Morgan, was shut down by authorities following police finding 57 bodies “not refrigerated and in various states of decomposition,” the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/08/06/decomposing-bodies-found-funeral-home-south-chicago-chapel-95th-street" target="_blank" ><u>Sun-Times previously reported</u></a>.</p><p>The Illinois Department of Financial and Professional Regulation revoked Johanna Morgan’s funeral director and embalmer’s license last week. Clark Morgan previously held a director and embalmer license, which was revoked in 2024. </p><p>The Illinois comptroller’s office permanently <a class="Link" href="https://illinoiscomptroller.gov/newsroom/press-releases/comptroller-mendoza-permanently-closes-heights-crematory-through-consent-order" target="_blank" ><u>shut down</u></a> Heights Crematory in Chicago Heights — <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago/2026/08/07/owners-of-far-south-side-funeral-home-have-history-of-mishandling-human-remains" target="_blank" ><u>which was also run by the Morgans</u></a> — last year after investigators found several improperly stored bodies and hundreds of cremated remains that “had never been returned to their families,” the office said in the statement.</p><p>In the wake of both investigations, Illinois Comptroller Susana Mendoza said she was “thankful” for a state law going into effect Jan. 1 that would allow her office to entries.title: The WNBA's gratitude police have a blind spot for Fever's Sophie Cunningham
entries.summary: <p>Sophie Cunningham owes <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky</a> guard Jacy Sheldon flowers.</p><p>That's her mom's position, anyway. Last season, after Sheldon poked Caitlin Clark in the eye, Cunningham answered with a flagrant foul that got her ejected — and went viral.</p><p>"'In fact, you should send her candy or flowers every month, because that moment has changed your life,'" Cunningham’s mom said.</p><p>Life has indeed gotten pretty good for Cunningham since then. Her reputation as Clark's "enforcer" brought more notoriety and endorsements. So Saturday, before a Sky-Fever game that featured its own viral flagrant on Cunningham, I asked Sheldon about that moment.</p><p>Had Cunningham ever apologized? Sheldon giggled, scoffed and shook her head.</p><p>"No."</p><p>Right. We all know Cunningham doesn't regret it. In trying to be polite, I'd asked the wrong thing.</p><p>The real question, by the standard applied to the rest of the league, is not whether she's sorry but whether she's grateful.</p><p>Is Cunningham grateful to Clark for the way their connection has raised her profile? Has she demonstrated the appropriate level of appreciation?</p><p>Funny thing. I don't hear anyone asking that. I guess Cunningham gets a pass.</p><p>Meanwhile, WNBA players have heard some version of that demand for two years: They need to be more grateful to Clark for the audience she brought to the league.</p><p>If you cover the WNBA, you hear it all the time. Starting in 2024, people would ask me some variation of the same questions, often presented as concern for the growth of the league.</p><p>Why don't the other players let Caitlin Clark score more?</p><p>Why don't they like her?</p><p>Why doesn't she have an "enforcer?"</p><p>None of it struck me as a threat to the league, so I tried to hear what people were really asking.</p><p>If I was being generous, I could hear people adjusting to the differences between the NBA and the WNBA.</p><p>A lot of new fans arrived from the men's side and were bothered by a far more physical league. There also isn't much of a tradition of a designated "enforcer" protecting a star player in the WBA, which I figured fans would get used to.</p><p>If I was being critical, though, I could hear some laziness.</p><p>Asking why players don't like Clark, or simply calling them "jealous," is a lot easier than grappling with the range of emotional reactions players might have to her popularity. After decades in which women's basketball stars, many of them Black and/or queer, never got their due, Clark's arrival could bring admiration and appreciation — but maybe some resentment, too.</p><p>But I don't think either dynamic fully explains the intensity and persistence of fan reactions to perceived "attacks" on Clark, which can produce days of knock-down, drag-out fights online.</p><p>So permit me a bit of armchair psychology.</p><p>I think when people ask, "Why don't other players like Clark?" there is an underlying fear that points back at them.</p><p>The gift and curse of sports is that we identify with our favorite players. We watch the game and suddenly we're the ones hitting the deep three or getting poked in the eye by Sheldon. That's just science. Look up mirror neurons if you're in the mood.</p><p>So if Clark is your hero, a slight against her can feel personal. Suddenly we're feeling that fundamental human anxiety about whether we are liked — but really, accepted.</p><p>That discomfort could be an opportunity to get vulnerable and talk about it. But we're cranky and overstimulated, so instead we turn to internet warfare.</p><p>The good news is I don't think this stands in the way of the league's success.</p><p>The basketball is too good. The players and storylines are too interesting. It's OK if we're a little new, a little lazy or a little overidentified with our favorite players.</p><p>Eventually, we can all calm down and enjoy it.</p><p>One dynamic does worry me, though. I see it where Cunningham's rising popularity meets the gratitude policing around Clark.</p><p>For some fans, complaining that WNBA players aren't grateful enough to Clark seems to bridge two impulses: newfound excitement about Clark and the Fever, and a desire to continue the longstanding tradition of diminishing the WNBA and its history.</p><p>To Clark's credit, she doesn't really play that mess.</p><p>She always talks about playing in the WNBA as a lifelong dream and about the players she watched growing up. And while Clark is not exactly at the tip of the league's progressive spear, she doesn't position herself in opposition to its spirit, either.</p><p>Cunningham offers something different. She rarely mentions how the league shaped her growing up — not once did it come up in the big ESPN profile on her. And she’s more willing to position herself against parts of its progressive culture, lately through her stance on transgender athletes in women's sports.</p><p>Maybe there’s a gift here: Cunningham helps nonprogressive fans feel seen in a league where they previously didn't. A bigger WNBA audience will necessarily include people with different politics.</p><p>But if Cunningham fandom gives people a way to cheer for the Fever while continuing to spit on the league? I think that’s corrosive.</p>

entries.title: Latest Matthew Boyd gem highlights Cubs’ arms in thick of playoff race: ‘Pitching is what drives things’
entries.summary: <p>KANSAS CITY, Mo. — Seven innings is getting to be the norm for <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" target="_blank" >Cubs</a> left-hander Matthew Boyd.</p><p>The front office <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/03/cubs-mlb-trade-deadline-jed-hoyer-top-prospects-trades-kevin-gausman-clay-holmes-ryan-zeferjahn-braxton-garrett-tyrone-taylor" target="_blank" >got aggressive at the trade deadline</a> and added two starters to the top of the rotation. But Boyd, a 2025 All-Star, is showing the Cubs <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/07/01/cubs-matthew-boyd-all-star-ace-starting-rotation-pitching-injuries-craig-counsell-pete-crow-armstrong-alex-bregman-thumbs-down" target="_blank" >already might have had an ace</a>, the type of pitcher they can be confident giving the ball for Game 1 of a playoff series.</p><p>Boyd’s latest gem was seven innings of two-run ball in the Cubs’ 10-2 drubbing Sunday of the Royals, another strong performance in a string of them since he returned from the injured list in late June. He has gone seven innings in three of his last four starts and has pitched into the seventh in five of his last six.</p><p>Since getting back on the mound after a nearly two-month layoff with a knee injury, he has a 2.43 ERA in nine starts.</p><p>‘‘He’s just been pitching so well since he’s come off the injured list and really been a big boost to what we’ve done in the starting rotation,’’ manager Craig Counsell said.</p><p>Even though Boyd has looked like an ace, he has been only one part of a collective starting effort that has been among the best in the majors for some time. Entering Sunday, the Cubs had a 3.31 ERA from their starters — the best in the National League and the third-best in the majors — since June 11.</p><p>With a challenging stretch of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/08/cubs-pete-crow-armstrong-17-games-17-days-ian-happ-homer-clay-holmes-debut-injury-royals" target="_blank" >17 games in 17 days</a> behind them, the Cubs can credit their rotation — with a 2.90 ERA — for driving the bus to a 12-5 record.</p><p>With Boyd and fellow left-handers Shota Imanaga and David Peterson joining forces with trade-deadline additions Kevin Gausman and Clay Holmes, the Cubs can be excited about what awaits in the rest of the regular season and into the playoffs.</p><p>‘‘There’s a lot of really good arms, a lot of experience,’’ Holmes said Sunday. ‘‘We can all make each other better and keep elevating each other.</p><p>‘‘At this time of the year and in the playoffs, pitching is what drives things. For us all to be at our best in this part of the year would be a fun thing to be a part of because of the potential here.’’</p><p>The weekend provided a look at the Cubs’ new-look rotation, with Gausman and Holmes making their debuts against the Royals. <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/07/cubs-kevin-gausman-starting-pitching-jed-hoyer-mlb-trade-deadline-royals-blue-jays" target="_blank" >Gausman was excellent</a>, going seven innings, while Holmes was rusty in his first start since hitting the IL with a fractured fibula in mid-May.</p><p>While Gausman already has earned rave reviews, Counsell drew comparisons between Holmes’ comeback and the one Boyd made earlier this season. While it might be a lot to expect anyone to do what Boyd has done, Holmes was stellar before getting hurt, with a 2.39 ERA in nine starts.</p><p>‘‘Man, he’s going to be great for us,’’ Boyd said of Holmes. ‘‘ ‘Gaus,’ what he can do with his [pitch] mix, it’s elite. . . . Seeing him in a Cubbie uniform doing that a few days ago was really awesome.</p><p>‘‘I’m grateful that they’re both Cubbies. It only makes us a better team. It’s really fun to pitch alongside them.’’</p><p>The starting staff is actually even deeper, finally looking at some depth after injuries stretched things to their limits earlier this summer.</p><p>Right-handers Colin Rea and Javier Assad have been <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/09/cubs-pitching-staff-colin-rea-bullpen-starting-rotation-playoffs-shelby-miller-injury-caleb-thielbar" target="_blank" >bumped to relief roles</a> by the arrivals of Gausman and Holmes, growing a group that could power the Cubs from the mound in the thick of a playoff race.</p><p>‘‘We’re very talented,’’ Boyd said. ‘‘Not only the five that we have now, but the seven, with C-Rea and Assad. They’re very much a part of this, too, and they’ve got us to where we are. . . . We really believe in this group, and we’ve been on a good run.’’</p><p>‘‘We’ve got a lot of depth now, which is good,’’ Rea said Sunday. ‘‘It’s hard to predict what’s going to happen, but I think they got the right pieces in here to set us up for success. We just have a group of guys who have a good idea of what they need to do and how to be successful. . . . We’re in a good spot.’’</p>

entries.title: Bears' defensive injuries in training camp show how thin their margin is this season
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> are entering scary territory in their secondary.</p><p>Injuries are piling up, and they’re searching the ends of their roster and free agents for answers. Issues like this aren’t a disaster with the season still more than a month away, but it’s an ominous sign of how precarious the plan is.</p><p>That’s a secondary, by the way, that has a lot on its shoulders already because the Bears don’t have a proven pass rush that could make cornerbacks’ jobs much easier.</p><p>The defensive star of practice Sunday was safety Xavier Woods with two interceptions and a thumping hit on tight end Colston Loveland. Woods, 31, was unsigned until Friday. Two days later he was making a case to be a Week 1 starter.</p><p>The Bears are in that situation because of thin depth across the board on defense, where talent development and acquisition have lagged behind the offense during general manager Ryan Poles’ rebuild.</p><p>At cornerback, they’ve got Jaylon Johnson, but they’re hoping for the best with Tyrique Stevenson and down to their third option at nickel as Kyler Gordon’s injury trouble continues. The Bears would love to have Terell Smith challenging Stevenson for a starting spot, as he has ever since they arrived as draft picks in 2023, but he’s hurt.</p><p>Without prized free-agent safety Coby Bryant, who is projected to be out until October, they moved Cam Lewis to his spot, but Lewis is injured, too — eliminating, for now, the Bears’ backup plan at two key positions.</p><p>Lewis, Smith and fellow defensive back Jaylon Jones were out again Sunday.</p><p>Cornerback has been a volatile position over Poles’ tenure.</p><p>He inherited a roster that had Johnson and virtually no one else who was starting-caliber, and by 2023 had flipped it to a good unit of Johnson and Stevenson, the No. 56 overall pick that year, on the outside with Gordon manning the slot.</p><p>Johnson has been outstanding aside from a major injury last season, but Stevenson has been all over the place and Gordon had three injuries last season, then got hurt again this offseason.</p><p>Those injuries, along with linebackers T.J. Edwards and D’Marco Jackson and defensive end Montez Sweat getting hurt, have left the defense in tatters. The Bears would have a brutal time missing such important pieces during the season.</p><p>For contrast, the offense has enough depth to withstand quite a few hits.</p><p>If the Bears lost three of their playmaking skill players for a stretch, for example, coach <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2025/09/01/the-bears-and-their-fans-needed-a-truth-teller-they-got-one-in-new-coach-ben-johnson" >Ben Johnson</a> would have plenty of alternatives.</p><p>Without top wide receiver Rome Odunze for the final five-regular season games, the Bears averaged 27 points down the stretch, and when running back D’Andre Swift missed the Bengals game, backup Kyle Monangai rushed for 176 yards. The offensive line, other than at left tackle, has backups who look capable of starting in a pinch.</p><p>The defense simply hasn’t been built as thoroughly, and that puts the onus on coordinator Dennis Allen to be a problem solver.</p><p>He managed admirably last season with the development of castoff Nahshon Wright into a starting cornerback when Jaylon Johnson was out of training camp and the midseason pickup of C.J. Gardner-Johnson to fill in for Gordon. Even still, the Bears’ defense was held together by a thread as it led the NFL in takeaways, but allowed the fourth-most yards and 10th-most points.</p><p>Allen said Sunday he’d rather deal with these injuries now than in the season, but, of course, that’s not how injuries work. This isn’t necessarily the only wave of them his defense will face, and the Bears would need a lot of quality players to emerge for them to survive something like this when it matters.</p>

entries.title: Bumped to bullpen by Cubs’ trade-deadline additions, Colin Rea gets time to prepare for possible playoff role
entries.summary: <p>KANSAS CITY, Mo. — The four innings <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" target="_blank" >Cubs</a> right-hander <b>Colin Rea</b> pitched Saturday might not have seemed terribly different from his usual day at the office.</p><p>For him, however, everything was different. Those innings came in relief.</p><p>‘‘When you’re starting . . . you can have a slow build-up to the game, so you can feel your stuff out,’’ Rea said Sunday. ‘‘Whereas coming out of the bullpen, you’ve got to be ready to go. You’re on from Pitch 1. There’s no easing into the game or getting a feel for stuff, like as a starter. That’s something I’ve got to work on.’’</p><p>Rea has shifted from the rotation — where he racked up the second-most starts as an injury fill-in — to the bullpen in the wake of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/03/cubs-mlb-trade-deadline-jed-hoyer-top-prospects-trades-kevin-gausman-clay-holmes-ryan-zeferjahn-braxton-garrett-tyrone-taylor" target="_blank" >the trade deadline</a>, when the Cubs added right-handers <b>Kevin Gausman</b> and <b>Clay Holmes</b> to the starting staff.</p><p>With the new guys in, some of the old guys had to move out. Rea and right-hander <b>Javier Assad</b> were bumped to depth pieces — good ones, considering their work helping an injury-ravaged staff stay afloat this summer.</p><p>Depth issues paved the way for the Cubs’ earlier-than-hoped playoff exit last fall. While Rea rather would be starting, a longer period of relieving before he might be asked to pitch out of the bullpen in October might prove to be helpful.</p><p>‘‘I view myself as a starter and have faith in myself that I can start at the major-league level,’’ he said. ‘‘But I think this is good moving forward, especially come postseason time. There’s a good chance, like last year, I would be in the bullpen anyway. This gives me time to really work on what we need to work on.</p><p>‘‘I might need to do things a little different in the bullpen. Now we have that time from now till the end of the season to figure out what that’s like.’’</p><p>Rea and Assad taking on new roles, coupled with the influx of more talent, makes <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/04/cubs-pitching-starting-rotation-mlb-trade-deadline-kevin-gausman-clay-holmes-jed-hoyer-craig-counsell-colin-rea-edward-cabrera-braxton-garrett" target="_blank" >the staff as a whole</a> much stronger.</p><p>‘‘The new additions, it’s going to be fun to watch those guys; I’m excited,’’ Rea said. ‘‘They’re veteran guys who know what they want to do, and I can pick their brains at the same time and translate it to help me.’’</p><h3>Miller time?</h3><p>Right-hander <b>Shelby Miller</b> started a rehab assignment with Triple-A Iowa.</p><p>The Cubs signed Miller, a veteran of 13 major-league seasons, to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/02/13/cubs-finalizing-multi-year-deal-with-reliever-shelby-miller-after-offseason-elbow-surgery" target="_blank" >a multiyear deal</a> in the spring as he worked his way back from elbow surgery, not expecting him to pitch much — if at all — in 2026.</p><p>Miller, who posted a 2.74 ERA in 48 relief appearances last season for the Diamondbacks and Brewers, has made impressive progress.</p><p>‘‘Shelby’s rehab and return to play, at this point, has gone as well as it possibly could,’’ manager <b>Craig Counsell</b> said. ‘‘We’ve got to a place that we probably didn’t anticipate getting to . . . when we signed him.</p><p>‘‘We’ve got steps to go here still, so I wouldn’t consider this like, ‘Yeah, Shelby Miller’s back.’ . . . His rehab’s going to be a little longer, and we have to be a little safer with his rehab, as well.’’</p><h3>Calling on Caleb</h3><p>Left-handed reliever <b>Caleb Thielbar</b> has struggled recently. His ERA has risen to 5.30, thanks to seven runs allowed in his last five outings. He also has allowed 10 home runs, a worrisome trend for one of the Cubs’ most counted-on relief arms.</p><p>‘‘I know Caleb’s going to have to get big outs still,’’ Counsell said, ‘‘and I’m going to continue to use him in big spots because he’s going to be our best matchup in some situations.’’</p>

entries.title: Noah Schultz still part of White Sox' plans this season, despite demotion
entries.summary: <p>Rookie left-hander Noah Schultz is still in the White Sox’ big-league plans this season, just not right now.</p><p>Pitching coach Zach Bove said the Sox expect Schultz, whom they optioned to Triple-A Charlotte on Saturday, to pitch for them later in the year and hopefully in the playoffs. With the team pushing for that playoff spot and Schultz struggling, the time was right to give him a reset.</p><p>“If you look back at the innings, the injuries over the years, this guy hasn’t had a full season,” Bove said Sunday before the series finale against the Guardians. “He’s 23 years old, has been a top prospect, all of that comes with it. But he’s still getting into his own. You saw that up here, the flashes of, ‘Man, this guy can be really good,’ and then some inconsistencies.”</p><p>Those flashes include four outings in which he allowed one run or fewer in at least five innings. Overall, Schultz has allowed 44 earned runs in 65 ⅓ innings (6.06 ERA).</p><p>Another issue is Schultz matching his career high in innings for a season (88 ⅓) with the one-third of an inning he threw Friday — though the short start was because of manager Will Venable mistakenly making a second mound visit.</p><p>“Noah’s obviously a big part of our future,” Bove said, “but use this time as a reset, work on some specific things, but also get used to the grind of a season, 130, 140 innings.”</p><p>What are those specific things?</p><p>“The slot’s gotten a little lower, a little scoopier, which then affects the four-seam [fastball], doesn’t have much ride,” Bove said. “I think getting the slot a little more upright, a little taller in the setup, adds [vertical break] to the four-seam. It helps the whole arsenal play out in that east-west range.”</p><p>Schultz, who will be in Charlotte’s rotation, seems more comfortable throwing side to side than up and down. But the Sox think he’ll miss more bats by having north-south options.</p><p>“It allows [pitches] to get above and below the barrel,” Bove said. “Having something that goes above the barrel with the four-seam and below the barrel with the slider, curveball, adds another element to the mix.”</p><h3>The Kay to his success</h3><p>Left-hander Anthony Kay has allowed two runs or fewer in seven of his last nine starts, a span in which he has a 2.96 ERA in 45 ⅔ innings. He allowed two runs in six innings Saturday against the Guardians, both coming in the sixth. Bove credits Kay’s changeup to his success.</p><p>“No. 1, being able to land it,” Bove said. “The guys have to respect that, which then makes that cutter, the four-seam up and in to the righties play up even more. And then being able to land the sweeper specifically.</p><p>“If he’s landing the changeup and the sweeper, I think it slows them down to make the four-seam and the cutter play up even more.”</p><h3>Notes</h3><p>Second baseman Chase Meidroth wasn’t in the lineup Sunday because his left wrist was bothering him. He was available off the bench and should be back in the lineup Tuesday for the series opener against the Reds at Rate Field.</p><p>• Right-handers Sean Burke and Luis Castillo are set to start the first two games of the Reds series. The starter for Thursday is to be determined. The Reds will counter with lefty Nick Lodolo, righty Rhett Lowder and lefty Andrew Abbott.</p><p>• The Sox have drawn 30,000-plus fans 19 times this season, one more than their total from 2023 to ’25. It’s their most since 2022 (20). entries.title: DiJonai Carrington's 'WHITE PRIVILEGE' post awaits response
entries.summary: <p>SEATTLE — Sky guard DiJonai Carrington's night ended after just three minutes Saturday. The story it started figures to run considerably longer.</p><p>Minutes after she was ejected from the game against the Fever for a Flagrant 2 foul on Indiana guard Sophie Cunningham, Carrington posted "WHITE PRIVILEGE" on Threads and tagged the Fever.</p><p>Sky coach Tyler Marsh said he learned of the post only when asked about it after the game.</p><p>"I have to get back to you on that because I'm just now hearing about that," Marsh said. "So, we'll handle that."</p><p>Carrington was not made available to reporters after the game, but she and Marsh will get questions Monday when the Sky play the Storm. The WNBA did not immediately respond to a request for comment.</p><p>Cunningham said she thought Carrington's foul was intentional and done for attention. She said in response to the Threads post:</p><p>"I think the league is taking care of that. This has nothing to do with race. Last year I did the same thing. I got kicked out, as I deserved to be kicked out. There's no reason to even play that card."</p><p>Last season, Cunningham committed a similar flagrant foul against Sky guard Jacy Sheldon in defense of Caitlin Clark. Cunningham acknowledged the parallel but said Carrington had "no reason" to get involved.</p><p>Before the game, Sheldon told the Sun-Times that Cunningham's flagrant foul from last season didn't stick with her.</p><p>"We don't focus on it," Sheldon said. "We don't care about it. We focus on the scout, to be honest."</p><p>Sky center Elizabeth Williams recalled Sheldon getting booed when the Sky played the Fever in Indiana.</p><p>"Which I'm like, 'Wow, we're booing Jacy?'" Williams said. "But no, I mean, we joke about it, but nothing serious. We're always going to have our teammates' backs."</p>

entries.title: Bears Training Camp Report, Day 10: WR Luther Burden sits with injury
entries.summary: <p>Breaking down the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a>’ training-camp practice Sunday:</p><h3><b>Burden out</b></h3><p>One day after limping off the practice field in the wake of a one-on-one drill against cornerback Tyrique Stevenson, wide receiver Luther Burden sat out with a groin injury. It’s unclear how long he will miss.</p><p>Another wide receiver got hurt during practice. Zavion Thomas, the rookie speedster from LSU, left early after appearing to favor his knee.</p><p>Linebacker D’Marco Jackson, left tackle Braxton Jones and defensive end Montez Sweat remained out. Kiran Amegadjie took the first-team snaps at left tackle.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Best thing I saw at <a href="https://x.com/hashtag/Bears?src=hash&ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">#Bears</a> practice was D’Andre Swift sliding after getting a first down to run the clock in a drill in which the offense was ahead late in the game. <a href="https://t.co/hNDjnqFhaM">pic.twitter.com/hNDjnqFhaM</a></p>— Patrick Finley (@patrickfinley) <a href="https://x.com/patrickfinley/status/2086567127218078040?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">August 9, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p></p><h3><b>The great indoors</b></h3><p>A thunderstorm that <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/08/09/bears-sunday-practice-delayed-by-lightning-near-halas-hall-fans-sent-home" target="_blank" >blew over Halas Hall</a> delayed practice by about an hour and a half and forced fans to leave. Playing inside the Walter Payton Center, quarterback Caleb Williams threw a 59-yard touchdown pass to wide receiver Jahdae Walker. The Bears finished with grueling a long-drive drill, in which the first-team players faced off against each other for 10 consecutive plays.</p><p>One downside to practicing indoors: Punter Tory Taylor booted a ball off the ceiling during a special-teams drill. The Bears went through the drill with one long snapper: Beau Gardner. They cut Luke Elkin, the other candidate for the job, before practice.</p><p></p><h3><b>‘Herd’ mentality</b></h3><p></p><p>Fox host Colin Cowherd, who has a home in Winnetka, chatted with general manager Ryan Poles and radio play-by-play man Jeff Joniak during practice.</p><p></p><h3><b>What’s next?</b></h3><p></p><p>The Bears will hold a walk-through at 11 a.m. at Stevenson High School in Lincolnshire.</p>
